title: Financial Agents Under Signed Mandates and Runtime Governance
subtitle: Agent identity, policy checks, human approvals and accountable execution
abstract: An agent may optimize or propose a transaction, but it acquires no legal authority merely by producing a convincing explanation. This report specifies a bounded financial-agent architecture that checks institutional identity, permitted actions, financial state, signed mandates, approvals and settlement evidence at the last actionable boundary.

evidence.heading: Runtime governance is becoming a distinct research practice
evidence.body: MAS published Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) in 2026, proposing industry approaches to agent authorization, oversight and decision records. This is a governance reference, not proof that an AI model is legally entitled to bind an institution. The more consequential the transfer, the more important it becomes to separate human or institutional delegation from an LLM-generated recommendation.

evidence.heading: Programmable finance increases the consequence of software actions
evidence.body: IMF work on tokenized finance discusses programmable infrastructures and their governance, while BIS research addresses financial transactions whose settlement and asset legs may execute within shared or coordinated systems. Software that can submit a valid payment can produce immediate financial effects; the runtime must therefore revalidate counterparty, amount, price, assets, approval conditions and available funds independently of the agent's textual reasoning.

evidence.heading: Risk cannot be outsourced to model explanations
evidence.body: The FSB's analysis of tokenization identifies operational risk and financial interconnections. Those considerations extend to autonomous workflows that combine APIs, market data, internal ledgers and issuer systems. A narrative audit log without authenticated policy versions, input provenance and real settlement evidence is inadequate to reconstruct why an economically relevant transaction occurred.

architecture.heading: Segregate authority from reasoning
architecture.body: Define a signed mandate containing the principal, maximum ticket, cumulative limits, permitted instruments, counterparties, settlement rails, price tolerance, time window and whether human approval is mandatory. An agent may recommend or negotiate within these bounds, but the actual execution gateway checks the mandate against independent state. Read-only research tools and privileged transaction tools should not share indistinguishable credentials.

architecture.heading: Bind consent to exact financial fields
architecture.body: Human approval must identify the amount, currency, payment destination, instrument, quote version, deadline and proposal hash. A materially changed transaction requires a new approval. Revoking the agent's authority or ending the window must block execution even if the model remains active. The model cannot grant itself larger limits or reinterpret policy text as permission.

architecture.heading: Close the evidence chain
architecture.body: Store the proposed action, signed mandate, validation decision, authorized approval, execution request, provider acknowledgment, finality proof and accounting event under a common economic ID. Distinguish blocked proposals from actual executed transfers. Exception recovery should retain the original event and any corrective entry; do not erase mistakes by editing an LLM transcript.

case.title: Synthetic treasury agent with a hard per-transfer limit
case.setup: A regulated treasury unit permits an agent to recommend USD transactions up to $120,000, requires a human signature above $75,000, and restricts permitted counterparties and rate deviations.
rows: Identity, instrument, counterparty and quote checked
Recognize final positions and fee journal
case.formula: Execute = ValidMandate ∧ InLimit ∧ EligibleCounterparty ∧ FreshQuote ∧ LiquidityAvailable ∧ (ApprovalRequired ⇒ ExactApproval).
case.interpretation: The agent's explanation supports operator review but cannot replace deterministic transaction authorization.

risks: Prompt injection
Untrusted market data directs the model to override its mandate.
Tool-output isolation and independent gateway checks.
Approval substitution
Payment destination changes after approval.
Approval binds to immutable exact terms.
Stale liquidity
Parallel transactions consume cash before the agent acts.
Fresh balance, reservations and final settlement checks.
tests: Attempt to alter destination and amount after approval; reject changed transactions.
Revoke authority before a scheduled instruction and verify the gateway blocks it.
Rebuild a completed execution from signed authorization to final bank and journal events.
conclusion: AFG should study runtime institutions, not unrestricted agents. Safe financial autonomy needs revocable mandates, deterministic control at execution and independently reconstructed outcomes.

title: Dual-Principal Agents and Negotiated Capital-Market Terms
subtitle: Independent buyer and seller mandates, counter-offers, consent and controlled DvP
abstract: Buyer and seller agents can negotiate a price or financing condition while maintaining separate interests and secret reservation values. Their negotiation transcript is not itself a securities contract or final settlement. This report designs a two-principal agent protocol with bounded offers, separate policy engines, human approval and a final execution gate.

evidence.heading: Delegation must be scoped by each institution
evidence.body: MAS SAFR proposes controls for agent identity, authority and consequential decisions. For a dual-principal scenario each participant should define its own signed mandate, approved instruments, price bounds, eligible counterparties, data sharing rules and execution powers. A marketplace coordinator must not silently merge a buyer's policy with the seller's or extract confidential reservation values.

evidence.heading: Negotiation and ownership are distinct economic stages
evidence.body: IMF tokenized-finance research and BIS project reports distinguish market arrangements, authorization and the final transfer of economic rights. A model can produce agreed indicative terms while the purchaser lacks funds, the seller lacks inventory or the recipient cannot legally hold the instrument. Those downstream gates must be checked after negotiation and before execution.

evidence.heading: Market oversight matters when software can act continuously
evidence.body: The FSB identifies interconnectedness and operational complexity in tokenized finance. An automated negotiation venue that permits opaque collusion, price manipulation, unbounded information sharing or unauthorized secondary transfers can amplify those risks. Keeping agent spaces independent and recording offers supports later assessment of the transaction's integrity.

architecture.heading: Two private agents with a neutral transcript
architecture.body: Each principal retains its own data store, mandate version, risk limits, preferences and log. The protocol publishes only authorized offer messages with proposal IDs, instrument, amount, currency, time and expiry. The coordinator timestamps and validates message order without obtaining unnecessary private reservation values. Human operators may inspect their own side's reasoning and the public dialogue.

architecture.heading: Feasibility is multidimensional
architecture.body: A price can fall within the buyer's ceiling and seller's floor yet remain infeasible for settlement. Verify available units, custody control, trading eligibility, currency acceptability, DvP route, FX cutoff and counterparty authorization. Price optimizers should use a total-value model including fees and settlement risk rather than maximize a single token quoted price.

architecture.heading: Approval precedes financial commitment
architecture.body: Separate tentative offer, counter-offer, indicative agreement, principal approval, binding instruction and settled delivery. Both parties must approve identical versioned terms before the settlement coordinator requests action. A subsequent change in payout account, quantity or price invalidates earlier approval unless the mandate explicitly permits that change.

case.title: Synthetic tokenized bond bilateral negotiation
case.setup: Buy-side agent seeks 100 authorized units. Maximum price $1,015 per unit; seller floor $1,000. DvP and regulated counterparty access are mandatory.
rows: Price feasible, not yet authorized execution
DvP only after valid rights and funding
case.formula: Feasible unit price interval = [seller minimum $1,000, buyer maximum $1,015]. At $1,008 × 100, gross amount is $100,800 before fees and FX.
case.interpretation: A negotiation outcome is a proposed term set, not proof of liquidity, market price fairness or ownership transfer.

risks: Leaked constraints
Coordinator observes private buyer ceiling and seller floor.
Private agent data spaces and disclosure policy.
Mutated approved terms
Destination or quantity changes after one signature.
Stable term hash and fresh mutual approval.
Unsettleable terms
Token units locked or holder ineligible.
Registrar and settlement gate before execution.
tests: Simulate ten rounds with independent mandates and no private-value sharing.
Inject an unauthorized price or account amendment after indicative agreement.
Compare negotiating surplus with net realized results after fees, FX and settlement success.
conclusion: Dual-principal negotiation is suitable for TSP-01 research if agent authority is explicit, parties remain independent and the final securities and monetary event obeys normal controls. AFG proposes terms; TSR, TLS and SPE establish executable reality.

title: Autonomous Treasury and Financial Intelligence That Reconcile
subtitle: Liquidity headroom, spending reservations, quote freshness and verified journal outcomes
abstract: Autonomous treasury must make decisions under cash, obligation and counterparty constraints that are not visible in a wallet balance alone. This report links AI route recommendations to deterministic liquidity reservations, settlement evidence and double-entry accounting. It distinguishes theoretical route optimization from actions that can safely discharge a financial obligation.

evidence.heading: Runtime controls are necessary for financial action
evidence.body: MAS SAFR recommends identifying agent authority, checking actions at runtime and preserving decision evidence. An agent can suggest an FX route, but a policy gateway must evaluate available cash and existing commitments immediately before execution. Delegating this to the language model's own memory leaves the institution exposed to stale balances, race conditions or prompt-injected exceptions.

evidence.heading: Liquidity and settlement have independent evidence
evidence.body: BIS Rialto, Meridian FX and Agorá examine combinations of FX conversion, synchronization and programmable payment infrastructure. Their prototypes reinforce why treasury must distinguish a quote, conditional hold, final transfer and beneficiary spendability. An autonomous agent can select among eligible routes, but only independently controlled financial systems can report actual reserves and final payments.

evidence.heading: Accounting verifies rather than narrates the outcome
evidence.body: IMF research on tokenized finance and FSB risk studies highlight the governance and operational dependencies of interconnected digital financial systems. A model-generated success message is not a bank statement, validated custody position or accounting posting. The system should record true executed amounts, fees, FX differences, reversals and unresolved claims under a canonical intent ID.

architecture.heading: Calculate spendable liquidity
architecture.body: Track settled cash, required operating buffer, reserved outgoing payments, collateral calls and permitted incoming liquidity. SpendableHeadroom = SettledAvailable − MinimumBuffer − ReservedPayments − CollateralHolds. Mark projected incoming funds and unredeemed settlement tokens separately rather than counting them as instantly spendable bank cash. Currency-specific positions and permissible conversion limits are necessary for cross-border treasury decisions.

architecture.heading: Proposal and reservation
architecture.body: An agent can rank eligible routes based on net proceeds, FX quote depth, funding time and counterparty risk. After a deterministic controller approves the route, reserve the cash against one immutable intent ID to prevent double spending by parallel agents. Confirm rate and destination before signing. Expired quotes or revoked mandates should cause reauthorization, not retries with stale terms.

architecture.heading: Settlement and journal closure
architecture.body: An executed payment should produce identifiable bank or token settlement evidence and matching journals for cash, payables, fees and any FX result. If payment fails, the controller releases reservations only when the actual rail's state allows it. Independent reconciliation should detect mismatched fees, stale settlements and payments whose beneficiary received a different amount from what the agent predicted.

case.title: Synthetic treasury headroom check
case.setup: Settled USD cash $300,000; required buffer $100,000; already reserved outgoing payments $70,000. The agent proposes an additional $180,000 conversion.
rows: Must not be used for discretionary transfer
case.formula: SpendableHeadroom = $300,000 − $100,000 − $70,000 = $130,000. Proposal $180,000 > $130,000, so policy must reject or resize it before any financial instruction.
case.interpretation: The agent does not create funding through optimization. Even a smaller instruction requires valid counterparty, quote, fee budget and approval checks.

risks: Double allocation
Parallel agent actions reserve the same cash.
Atomic reservation keyed by settlement intent.
Pending funds mistaken as available
Unsettled token receipt counts as bank liquidity.
Rail-specific finality and usability labels.
Journal omission
Payment settles but fees or liability reduction are not posted.
Independent provider statement and accounting reconciliation.
tests: Run simultaneous proposals against shared treasury cash and require correct total reservation.
Simulate partial FX fill and late bank settlement, preserving paid and reserved amounts.
Audit full chain from agent proposal and signed mandate to bank evidence and final journal entries.
conclusion: AFG is most valuable when financial intelligence is coupled to true balances, mandate controls and settled evidence. Autonomous treasury should be a governed decision-to-journal process rather than an unconstrained portfolio agent.
